entries.topicDescription: Making HTTP requests and handling APIs with URLSession and modern patterns.

tips.title: URLSession with async/await is clean and simple
tips.content:
URLSession gained async/await overloads in iOS 15. You can
fetch data, download files, or upload content with a single
await call — no delegates or completion handlers needed.

The async data(from:) method returns both the Data and the
URLResponse. Always check the HTTP status code before
decoding the response body.

Combine this with JSONDecoder for a complete networking
layer in just a few lines. Mark your network functions
as async throws for clean error propagation.

For more complex needs (background downloads, auth challenges),
you'll still need URLSessionDelegate, but most REST API calls
are beautifully simple with async/await.

tips.title: Codable makes JSON parsing type-safe
tips.content:
Swift's Codable protocol (Encodable + Decodable) maps JSON
to Swift types automatically. The compiler synthesizes the
implementation when all properties are themselves Codable.

Use CodingKeys to map JSON field names to Swift property names.
This handles snake_case to camelCase conversion and renaming
without manual parsing.

For nested JSON, create nested Codable structs that mirror
the JSON structure. Use optional properties for fields that
may be missing.

JSONDecoder has strategies for common transformations:
.convertFromSnakeCase for key decoding, .iso8601 for dates,
and custom strategies for anything else.

tips.title: Build a robust API layer with request interceptors
tips.content:
Production apps need more than raw URLSession calls. You
need authentication headers, retry logic, logging, and
consistent error handling.

Build a thin API layer that intercepts requests to add
auth tokens, logs responses for debugging, and retries
on transient failures (network timeouts, 5xx errors).

Use URLRequest to customize headers, HTTP method, and body.
Create a protocol for your API endpoints so each one
declares its path, method, and expected response type.

This pattern scales well: adding a new endpoint is just a
new enum case or struct, and cross-cutting concerns like
auth and logging are handled in one place.
